content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Your First C# Script
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Your First C# Script

Create a MonoBehaviour, run initialization and per-frame logic, and inspect Console output to confirm behavior.

Time: ~10 minutes
In this lesson
Create scripts, attach to a GameObject, and watch lifecycle logs.
Why it matters
Scripts give GameObjects behavior and are the core of game logic in Unity.
Coming up
Start vs Update, Debug.Log, and common mistakes to avoid.
Visual concept
Script asset
Scripts folder → Create → C# Script. Name file exactly to match the public class inside.
Attach to GameObject
Create an empty GameObject named ScriptHost, then add your script as a component to run its lifecycle.
Key Takeaway

A Unity script must inherit from MonoBehaviour and the file name must match the public class name so Unity can add it as a component and call Start and Update.

Starter code preview
using System.Collections;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using UnityEngine;

public class MyFirstScript : MonoBehaviour
{
    // Start is called before the first frame update
    void Start()
    {
        Debug.Log("Hello from Start!");
    }

    // Update is called once per frame
    void Update()
    {
        Debug.Log("Hello from Update!");
    }
}
Explore Key Topics
Create script
Organize in a Scripts folder and name the file carefully.
Lifecycle
Start runs once, Update runs every frame—use them accordingly.
Debugging
Use Debug.Log and the Console to confirm execution order and catch errors.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will perform four core tasks with confidence. First, you'll create a new C# script asset inside the Unity Project window and organize it inside a Scripts folder so your codebase stays tidy. Second, you'll attach that script to a GameObject so Unity can run it as a component. Third, you'll inspect and explain the structure of a MonoBehaviour-derived class: why using statements matter, where the public class declaration goes, and why inheritance from MonoBehaviour enables component behavior. Fourth, you'll write simple Debug. Log statements and run the scene to confirm that Start and Update execute as expected. Each skill is practical: creating and naming the file correctly prevents attach errors, attaching to a GameObject makes the code actually run, understanding the class structure avoids syntax errors, and logging helps you verify runtime flow. These are foundational skills that get you from clicking in the Editor to observing live behavior in Play mode.

screens.title: Creating and organizing a script asset
screens.narratorSegment: Creating your first script begins in the Project window. The practical habit to form is organization: create a folder named Scripts first, then create each new C# script inside it. This keeps code separate from assets like textures and scenes, making it easier to find behavior when your project grows. When you create a C# script, Unity generates a. cs file that will open in your IDE. Important rule: the filename must exactly match the public class name inside the file. If the file is named MyFirstScript. cs, then the class must be public class MyFirstScript. If those names differ, Unity will show an error when you try to attach the script and the component won't be available in the Add Component list. A common misconception is thinking you can rename either the file or the class independently; both must match. Practice: create Scripts → right-click Create → C# Script → name it LoggerScript. Open it in your IDE and confirm the public class line matches the filename. This simple discipline prevents a lot of attach-time frustration. Creating and organizing a script asset means always keep the .cs file name identical to the public class name so unity recognizes the script as a component.. In practical terms, make a scripts folder and add a new c# script with a descriptive name. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Creating and organizing a script asset
Process

Create folder → Create script → Name carefully

  1. Create a folder named Scripts in the Project window to store code.
  2. Inside Scripts, right-click → Create → C# Script to generate a .cs file.
  3. Name the file with a descriptive identifier like LoggerScript, matching the class name inside.
  4. Double-click the file to open it in your IDE and verify the public class line matches the filename.
Example
If file is LoggerScript.cs, the class must be public class LoggerScript.
Common mistake
Renaming the file but not the class, which causes "class cannot be found" errors when attaching.
Visual check
Project window (illustrative)
Scripts/
LoggerScript.cs
PlayerController.cs
Why it matters
Matching names ensures Unity can map the file to a component class so you can attach and run it. Skipping this prevents components from being added and wastes time troubleshooting.

screens.title: What is MonoBehaviour?
screens.narratorSegment: MonoBehaviour is the special base class in Unity that gives your scripts life inside the engine. When your public class inherits from MonoBehaviour, Unity treats it as a component you can attach to GameObjects. That inheritance provides access to core features like the lifecycle callbacks, coroutines, access to the GameObject and Transform properties, and integration with the Editor's component system. In practice this means you can write code like Start and Update and Unity will call those methods at the right time. A common misconception is thinking any C# class will automatically run in Unity; only classes deriving from MonoBehaviour can be attached and participate in the game loop. Another important point: MonoBehaviour methods are instance methods on the component attached to a GameObject, not static engine callbacks that run globally. This lets each GameObject hold its own state in fields and react independently. Understanding MonoBehaviour is key because it frames how you structure behavior and where you store per-object data. What is MonoBehaviour? means monobehaviour allows a class to function as a unity component, access gameobject state, and receive lifecycle callbacks like start and update.. In practical terms, why your script inherits from monobehaviour and what that enables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › What is MonoBehaviour?
Definition

MonoBehaviour explained

A base class provided by Unity that makes a C# class attachable to GameObjects and able to receive special callbacks during the game loop.

Provides
  • Lifecycle callbacks (Start, Update, OnEnable, etc.)
  • Access to component methods and properties like gameObject and transform
  • Ability to start coroutines and interact with the Editor component system
Misconception
Not every C# class runs in Unity. Only classes inheriting from MonoBehaviour become attachable components and participate in the game loop.
Analogy
Think of MonoBehaviour as a plugin interface that tells Unity, "This class expects to be hosted on a GameObject and to run with the engine." Without that interface, the class is inert in the Editor.
Key takeaway
Derive from MonoBehaviour when the class should be a component that Unity manages and calls over time.

screens.title: Boilerplate script structure
screens.narratorSegment: When you open a newly created script in your IDE you'll see a small but important structure. At the top are using statements such as using UnityEngine; which bring engine types into scope so you don't have to fully qualify them. Next is the public class declaration that must match the filename and include : MonoBehaviour to enable component behavior. Inside the class you'll typically find method stubs like Start and Update. Start is intended for one-time setup and runs once when the component becomes enabled before the first frame update. Update runs every frame and is used for per-frame checks or changes. A common mistake is putting heavy initialization or file input and output inside Update; that can cause performance problems because Update's frequency equals the frame rate. Another small point: comments in the boilerplate remind you what each method does; don't delete Start if you rely on it. Reading these parts every time helps you avoid naming and placement issues. Boilerplate script structure means boilerplate contains using statements, a public class inheriting monobehaviour, and lifecycle stubs. keep initialization in start and continuous work in update.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Boilerplate script structure
Code Walkthrough

Standard C# script template

using System.Collections;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using UnityEngine;

public class MyFirstScript : MonoBehaviour
{
    // Start is called before the first frame update
    void Start()
    {
        Debug.Log("Hello from Start!");
    }

    // Update is called once per frame
    void Update()
    {
        Debug.Log("Hello from Update!");
    }
}
Explanation
  • using UnityEngine; exposes Unity types like GameObject and Debug.
  • public class ... : MonoBehaviour makes the class a Unity component.
  • Start() runs once for setup; ideal for getting references or initial values.
  • Update() runs every frame; use for input checks and movement, but avoid expensive work here.
Pro tip
If you don't need Update, remove or comment it out to avoid empty calls every frame. Performance gains add up.

screens.title: Attach the script to a GameObject
screens.narratorSegment: Attaching a script is how you tell Unity to run it on a specific GameObject. Start by creating an empty GameObject in the Hierarchy—name it ScriptHost or GameManager for global logic. Select that GameObject, then either drag the script from the Project window onto the Inspector or click Add Component and search for the script name. If the script doesn't appear in Add Component, check that the filename and class name match and that there were no compile errors in the Console. Once attached, the fields you expose as public or serialized will appear in the Inspector and you can tweak values at runtime. When you press Play, Unity enables the component and calls Start once, followed by Update every frame. A misconception to avoid is assuming the script will run if it's present in the Project; it must be attached to an active GameObject. Also ensure the component is enabled in the Inspector; disabled components do not receive Start or Update calls until re-enabled. Attach the script to a GameObject means a script won't execute unless it is attached to an active gameobject and the class name matches the file name.. In practical terms, create a host gameobject and add your script as a component. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Start() vs Update()
screens.narratorSegment: Start and Update serve distinct roles in a MonoBehaviour lifecycle and picking the right one matters for correctness and performance. Start is called once when the component is enabled, immediately before the first frame update. Put initialization there: set initial variables, cache references to other components, or spawn starting objects. Update runs every frame, which makes it suitable for reading input, moving characters, or updating animations. The difference is frequency: Start runs once; Update runs repeatedly and its cost scales with frame rate. A common error is performing heavy setup inside Update, which wastes C P U and may cause unpredictable behavior. Another pitfall is relying on initialization in Start from another component that hasn't run its Start yet; in those cases use Awake, OnEnable, or explicit initialization order. For simple tasks: initialize state in Start and perform repeated checks and movement in Update. Ask yourself: does this work need to occur repeatedly, or is it a one-time setup? That question will guide your choice. Start() vs Update() means use start for one-time setup and update for frame-by-frame behavior; avoid expensive operations inside update to protect performance.. In practical terms, when to use one-time initialization and when to use per-frame logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Start() vs Update()
Start()

One-time initialization

Called once before the first frame update when the component is enabled. Ideal for getting references and setting initial state.

Example
Set player health to 100 and cache Rigidbody reference.
Update()

Per-frame logic

Runs every frame. Use for input polling, movement, and state checks that must happen continuously.

Common mistake
Putting expensive initialization or file access inside Update, which hurts frame rate and responsiveness.
Check your understanding
If you need to set an initial position based on a saved file, read the file in Start and apply the position once; if you need to poll input to move the character every frame, do that in Update.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Debug.Log and Console
Code example
private float timer = 0f;
public float logInterval = 2f; // Log every 2 seconds

void Start()
{
    Debug.Log("LoggerScript has started on " + gameObject.name + "!");
}

void Update()
{
    timer += Time.deltaTime;
    if (timer >= logInterval)
    {
        Debug.Log("LoggerScript is updating...");
        timer = 0f;
    }
}

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › LoggerScript Activity
Starter code
using UnityEngine;

public class LoggerScript : MonoBehaviour
{
    private float timer = 0f;
    public float logInterval = 2f; // Log every 2 seconds

    void Start()
    {
        Debug.Log("LoggerScript has started on " + gameObject.name + "!");
    }

    void Update()
    {
        timer += Time.deltaTime;
        if (timer >= logInterval)
        {
            Debug.Log("LoggerScript is updating...");
            timer = 0f;
        }
    }
}
Steps to run

  3. Create an empty GameObject named ScriptHost and attach LoggerScript.
  4. Press Play and open the Console. Observe the Start message once and Update messages every 2 seconds.

screens.title: Performance considerations for Update()
screens.narratorSegment: Update runs once per frame, so anything you place there executes frequently. That makes Update a sensitive place for performance. Expensive operations such as file input and output, heavy allocations, complex queries, or large loops should not run inside Update. Another practical technique is to disable components when they are not needed, or to gate logic behind state checks so Update exits quickly most frames. Always profile if performance is a problem. The core rule: keep Update lean—do the minimum work required each frame and move costly tasks to less frequent contexts. Why it matters

Because Update runs every frame, even small inefficiencies multiply quickly. Poorly placed code here can drop your frame rate.

  • Avoid file I/O, allocation-heavy loops, and frequent logging inside Update.
  • Use Start for setup and coroutines or timers to spread work across time.

Disable components

When a script fails to attach or run, the Unity Console is your first stop. Typical messages include compile errors with file and line numbers, or a warning that the script class cannot be found. A mismatched filename and public class name will present as a class-not-found error when trying to add the component. Syntax errors like missing semicolons or braces show up with compile messages that tell you which file and line to inspect. If you get a class-not-found error, open the. cs file and confirm the public class line exactly matches the filename. If you see compile errors, fix them in the IDE and save. Another issue is forgetting to attach the script: having the. cs file in the Project does nothing unless it's on an active GameObject. Finally, disabled components won't run; check the enabled toggle in the Inspector. The Console will guide you; read messages carefully instead of guessing. Systematic diagnosis—identify the message, open the referenced file, fix, save, and re-run—resolves most problems quickly. Update runs once per frame, so anything you place there executes frequently. That makes Update a sensitive place for performance. Expensive operations such as file input and output, heavy allocations, complex queries, or large loops should not run inside Update. Instead, perform heavy initialization once in Start or spread work across frames using coroutines or timed intervals. A specific concern is uncontrolled logging: Debug. Log in Update will flood the Console and can dramatically slow the Editor or build. Use a timer to limit logs to a few seconds and remove logs once debugging is complete. Another practical technique is to disable components when they are not needed, or to gate logic behind state checks so Update exits quickly most frames. Always profile if performance is a problem. The core rule: keep Update lean—do the minimum work required each frame and move costly tasks to less frequent contexts. Second, Start is called once for initialization and Update is called every frame for continuous logic; choose the correct place to avoid logic or performance bugs. Third, use Debug.
